slides.1.question: When is the best time for fortification (adding grape spirit) in Port production?
slides.1.options.1: Immediately after the grapes are pressed
slides.1.options.2: When natural alcohol reaches 7–8% (about 2–3 days into fermentation)
slides.1.explanation: Port is fortified with 77% grape spirit when fermentation has reached about 7–8% natural alcohol, halting fermentation and retaining 80–120 g/L residual sugar, with a final alcohol of 19–22%. The earlier the fortification, the sweeter the wine (Vintage); the later, the drier (some Tawny).
slides.2.question: What is the greatest advantage of traditional Lagar treading over a modern Autovinificator?
slides.2.options.1: The weight of human feet is moderate and does not crush the seeds, extracting fine tannins and rich colour
slides.2.explanation: The key advantage of the Lagar: the weight of human feet breaks the skins without crushing the seeds (which contain harsh, green tannins). In a fermentation period of only 2–3 days, Lagar treading maximises colour (anthocyanin) extraction while keeping tannins fine, making it the essential method for top Vintage Port.
slides.3.question: What is the main difference between "unfiltered LBV" and "Vintage Port"?
slides.3.options.0: They are identical, just with different names
slides.3.options.1: LBV is bottled after 4–6 years in cask (later); Vintage Port is bottled after 2 years in cask (shorter) but is made only in officially declared top years
slides.3.options.2: LBV uses only Touriga Nacional, Vintage uses several varieties
slides.3.options.3: Vintage Port is unfiltered, while LBV must be filtered
slides.3.explanation: LBV (Late Bottled Vintage): a single vintage, bottled after 4–6 years in cask, and can be made in years that are not officially declared. Vintage Port: made only in the best officially declared years (roughly every 3–4 years), bottled after only 2 years in cask, then aged 20–50 years in bottle to reach its peak.
slides.4.question: What does the "30 Years Tawny" label mean?
slides.4.options.0: Grapes harvested by the estate in 1994 (30 years ago)
slides.4.options.1: The oldest wine in the blend is 30 years old
slides.4.options.2: A blend of wines of various ages that shows the oxidative complexity of a "style age of about 30 years"
slides.4.options.3: A further 30 years of ageing in bottle
slides.4.explanation: The age statement on Tawny Port (10/20/30/40 years) represents the "style age" of the blend, not a specific harvest year. The blender mixes Tawnies of anywhere from 15 to 45 years so that the finished wine matches the style of "30 Years" in colour, aroma (coffee・aged orange peel・rum) and palate.
slides.5.question: How long must Madeira made by the Canteiro method age in oak casks at a minimum to be labelled Frasqueira (top Vintage Madeira)?
slides.5.explanation: Frasqueira (Vintage Madeira) is Madeira's highest grade. It must use the natural Canteiro method (not Estufagem), be aged in oak casks for at least 20 years, and be a single vintage. This is an official IVBAM rule. After bottling it can continue to age for 50–100 years.
slides.6.question: Of the four Madeira varieties, which is planted at the lowest altitude (0–200m) and is the sweetest?
slides.6.explanation: Malvasia (Malmsey) is planted in the warm coastal zone at Madeira's lowest altitude (0–200m) and has the highest sugar levels, making a very sweet style (about ≥100 g/L, Doce). Despite the high sweetness, Madeira's naturally high acidity stops it cloying, with honey・apricot・tropical fruit aromas, and it is the most popular Madeira style on the market.
slides.7.question: What is the most fundamental difference in production between Bairrada Espumante and Vinho Verde's light sparkle?
slides.7.options.0: Both use the traditional method; the difference is in the variety
slides.7.options.1: Bairrada uses the traditional method (secondary fermentation in bottle), while Vinho Verde keeps natural CO₂ in the tank
slides.7.options.2: Vinho Verde uses the Charmat method, while Bairrada keeps natural bubbles
slides.7.explanation: Bairrada Espumante uses the traditional method (Método Clássico), with secondary fermentation in the bottle, pressure of about 6 bar and 9–36 months on lees. Vinho Verde's light sparkle traditionally comes from CO₂ produced as a by-product of malolactic fermentation, and today is mostly injected directly, at pressure below 1 bar. They are completely different processes.
slides.8.question: Why have Portugal's old Ramisco vines (Colares) never been attacked by phylloxera, and why do they still have own-rooted (ungrafted) vines of over a century old?
slides.8.options.1: Portuguese law forbids phylloxera from entering
slides.8.options.2: The sand of the dunes prevents phylloxera from surviving in it, so it never spread to Colares
slides.8.options.3: Atlantic sea winds stopped phylloxera from spreading
slides.8.explanation: Colares' Ramisco vines are planted in the deep sand of Atlantic coastal dunes, where phylloxera cannot survive in loose sand, so the phylloxera that destroyed the European wine industry in the 19th century never affected Colares. The vines kept their original roots, and some are over a century old, making them the world's most precious living fossils of wine.
slides.9.question: What is the main winemaking advantage of the Balseiro (a traditional large old oak cask) over a 225L new French Barrique?
slides.9.options.1: Slow micro-oxidation that softens tannins without adding oak vanilla or smoky flavour, preserving the purity of variety and terroir
slides.9.options.2: It makes the wine age faster
slides.9.explanation: The Balseiro (large old cask) lets the wine micro-oxidise slowly through the tiny pores of the staves, softening tannins and making the palate smoother, but adds no oak aroma at all (the wood has been used many times and its oak flavour is exhausted). This fully preserves the violet florals of Touriga Nacional and the minerality of Encruzado, and is a key tool of traditional Portuguese terroir expression.
slides.10.question: Why can vine roots reach 10–20 metres deep in Portugal's Douro schist (Xisto) soil?
slides.10.options.0: Schist is very soft and roots penetrate easily
slides.10.options.2: Schist has vertical layered fissures, and vine roots penetrate down along them to find deep groundwater
slides.10.options.3: Schist soil is especially moist, so roots do not need to go down for water
slides.10.explanation: The most important physical property of Douro schist is its vertical layered fissures. Vine roots penetrate down along these natural cracks, as deep as 10–20 metres, in search of deep groundwater, keeping up the water supply during summer drought and also drawing up deep minerals. This is the source of the minerality and complexity of Douro wines.
slides.11.question: Which characteristic of the wine does the "3–6 months of maceration on fresh grape skins" after fortification in Moscatel de Setúbal mainly increase?
slides.11.options.2: The intensity of Muscat floral aromas (terpene aroma compounds)
slides.11.explanation: Moscatel de Setúbal's unique maceration on fresh grape skins (a step absent from other fortified wines) lets the natural terpene aroma compounds in the skins dissolve into the wine in large quantities, greatly increasing the intensity of the Muscat and orange blossom aromas. This is the most striking aromatic feature of Moscatel de Setúbal and what sets it most apart from other sweet wines.
slides.12.question: What is the most fundamental difference between Pétillant Naturel (Pét-Nat) and traditional-method sparkling wine (Bairrada Espumante)?
slides.12.options.1: Pét-Nat has only one fermentation (not finished when bottled), while the traditional method has two (an additional secondary fermentation)
slides.12.options.2: Pét-Nat has more and longer-lasting bubbles
slides.12.options.3: Pét-Nat must be disgorged (dégorgement), while the traditional method does not need to be
slides.12.explanation: Pét-Nat (Pétillant Naturel) uses the ancestral method (Méthode Ancestrale): the wine is bottled before the first fermentation has finished, and yeast remaining in the bottle consumes residual sugar to produce CO₂, so there is only one fermentation throughout, usually leaving a slight yeast sediment. The traditional method (Bairrada Espumante) has two fermentations: after the first is complete, a tirage liqueur is added for secondary fermentation in bottle, and the wine is finally disgorged (dégorgement).
